summary:
AstroCare is a browser-based health monitoring prototype that helps astronauts record health indicators, understand changes over time, and identify information that needs medical review during long-duration space missions.

The application combines heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, sleep duration, mood, and reported symptoms in a visual dashboard. An interactive body explorer explains how these indicators relate to different areas of the body, while historical charts and explainable alerts help users review their measurements in context.

AstroCare addresses the challenge of supporting health awareness when communication with Earth may be delayed or unavailable. It stores records locally, includes offline access after initial setup, and allows users to export health summaries for later review.

NASA’s Human Research Program resources informed the project’s educational content and design. The prototype uses synthetic demonstration data and illustrative assessment rules. It does not diagnose medical conditions or prescribe treatment; clinical validation would be required before operational use.
details:
Project overview

AstroCare is an astronaut health monitoring prototype designed to make health information easier to record, interpret, and review during space missions.

The application brings measurements, symptoms, historical trends, and educational guidance into one interface. Its main workflow allows a user to record a check-in, review the results, understand why a finding was highlighted, and prepare a report.

The problem

Long-duration missions expose astronauts to physical and psychological challenges. NASA’s Human Research Program identifies five major hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile or closed environments.

These hazards make health awareness and access to understandable information important. A collection of measurements alone is insufficient if users cannot tell when the data was recorded, whether it is comparable with earlier readings, or what requires further attention.

AstroCare explores how a visual monitoring tool can support this process while recognizing the limitations of a student-built prototype.

Our solution

AstroCare provides a local-first workspace for recording and reviewing health information. Its interface displays individual indicators and their context rather than combining them into an unsupported overall health score.

The application distinguishes between measurements that fall within its demonstration ranges, findings that need review, urgent reported symptoms, and information that is missing or outdated.

Main features

Health dashboard

The dashboard displays the latest heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, body temperature, sleep duration, and mood rating. Each indicator includes its unit, measurement time, and an explanatory status.

Daily check-in

Users can enter available measurements, select resting or after-activity context, report symptoms, and add notes. Unavailable measurements can remain blank. Validation checks help prevent incomplete blood-pressure pairs, invalid values, and future measurement times.

Interactive body explorer

A clickable body diagram connects body regions with relevant measurements and educational explanations. Users can explore wellbeing, circulation, abdominal symptoms, muscles and bones, and whole-body health.

The interface explicitly identifies functions that are not assessed. For example, completing an exercise task does not establish bone density or muscle strength.

Historical trends

Charts show up to 14 recent check-ins for a selected indicator. A history table provides exact values, units, timestamps, and measurement context. Heart-rate charts include a saved resting baseline for comparison.

Explainable alerts

A transparent rule-based assessment module generates findings with an explanation and suggested next step. Demonstration rules cover out-of-range readings, outdated data, repeated changes from the saved heart-rate baseline, and potentially serious reported symptoms.

After-activity heart rate is excluded from resting-range and resting-baseline assessments. Urgent symptom flags remain relevant even when other measurements fall within the demonstration ranges.

Users can acknowledge findings, but acknowledgement does not remove them or mark them as medically resolved.

Guidance and routine tracking

The guidance page explains measurement preparation, status meanings, prototype rules, and research sources. A daily checklist supports check-ins, reviewing guidance, and reviewing planned exercise.

The checklist rewards completion through progress tracking rather than rewarding particular health readings.

Local storage and offline support

Records are stored in the browser using IndexedDB. A service worker caches application assets so the application can support offline access after initial setup.

The prototype does not transmit health information, connect to medical devices, or automatically contact ground support.

Reports

Users can export the selected profile’s records as CSV or JSON, or print a summary and save it as a PDF through the browser. Reports include measurements and relevant context. Downloading a report does not send it to a clinician.

How the application works

1. The user selects a fictional crew profile.

2. The user enters available measurements, symptoms, and context.

3. Input validation checks the submission.

4. The application saves the check-in locally.

5. The assessment module evaluates the latest information and relevant recent history.

6. The dashboard and trend charts update.

7. The user reviews explanations, acknowledges findings, and exports a report if needed.

Two fictional profiles demonstrate separation of crew records. Synthetic routine and changing-trend scenarios allow judges to explore the system without entering personal health information.

Technology used

- HTML and CSS for the interface and responsive layout.

- JavaScript modules for interactions, validation, assessment, and reporting.

- SVG for the body illustration and charts.

- IndexedDB for browser-based data storage.

- A service worker for offline asset caching.

- Node.js for a lightweight local development server.

- Node.js’s built-in test runner for automated assessment tests.

The project runs locally in Visual Studio Code without external package dependencies or API keys.

Use of space-agency resources

NASA resources informed the project’s understanding of spaceflight hazards, preventive health monitoring, operational constraints, and the value of onboard guidance.

These resources are used as research and educational references. They are not presented as the source of the application’s synthetic records or illustrative thresholds.

Testing and current status

The prototype’s eight automated assessment and validation tests passed. These cover valid entries, missing information, blood-pressure consistency, urgent symptoms, stale measurements, activity context, repeated baseline changes, and invalid inputs.

The local server was also checked and successfully served the application files.

Full browser testing, including visual rendering, persistence, downloads, and offline behaviour, remains to be completed on the team’s target devices. An acceptance checklist is included with the project.

Limitations

AstroCare is a research prototype, not a clinically validated medical device. Its assessment thresholds are illustrative and are not NASA-approved medical protocols.

The application does not diagnose illness, prescribe medication, assess radiation injury, measure bone density, interpret ultrasound images, or determine fitness for duty.

The prototype has no authentication or application-level encryption and should be demonstrated using fictional data only. It does not include cloud synchronization, sensor integration, or medical messaging.

Future development

Future work could include professionally reviewed assessment rules, validated device integration, stronger access controls, encrypted storage, secure communication workflows, and usability evaluation with appropriate domain experts.

The immediate goal is to demonstrate an understandable monitoring workflow that connects measurements, context, explanations, and next actions.
